facts.fact: Lũa kim sa tùng is sold as aquarium and aquascape driftwood, in 1 kg lots, in the shop's 'Lũa Thủy Sinh' category.
The seller says the wood is sa tùng, but gives no botanical name.
It is described as an upright, sturdy piece that looks like an old tree.
The seller says its shape is natural, with no cutting and joining and no reworking.
Aqua Mart says its lũa kim sa tùng is made from selected branches of sa tùng wood.
Aqua Mart describes it as having an open, natural form, like an old tree standing upright in the tank.
Aqua Mart lists it beside other driftwood types: Lũa Hải Sơn Tùng, Lũa linh sam, Lũa rễ rừng and Lũa đỗ quyên.
Bống Vàng sells Lũa Kim sa tùng by weight (1 kg) and says it is made from sa tùng wood.
Brothers Concept sells it in two forms: 'cổ thụ gốc' (base/trunk pieces) and 'cổ thụ nhánh' (branch pieces).
Brothers Concept describes the branch version as looking like an old, upright tree, with a fully natural shape that has not been cut, joined or reworked.
A terrarium shop describes Lũa Kim Sa Tùng as the hard core left after the bark and softer wood of a Sa Tùng (Juniperus chinensis) tree weather away.
The same terrarium shop describes twisting, naturally curving shapes, warm, muted colours and swirling grain.
The terrarium shop says the wood comes from East Asia, including China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam.
The terrarium shop calls the wood durable and resistant to termites and rot, but gives no evidence.
The seller says sa tùng wood does not release colour into the water.
Bống Vàng says sa tùng wood does not fade or bleed colour into the water.
Brothers Concept says you will not see sa tùng wood leach colour into the water.
A general Vietnamese driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng says tannin is released early on and is the main cause of yellow water.
A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng says tannin softens water and gently lowers pH, but gives no figures.
A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng says new wood often grows a white mold or film, which usually fades as the tank stabilises.
The seller says the wood is sold already processed: boiled, with the bark scraped off.
Brothers Concept says its sa tùng driftwood is boiled until cooked through and then scraped clean of bark before sale.
For terrarium use, the terrarium shop says to rinse the wood under running water to remove dust and debris.
A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng says to scrub with a stiff brush to remove dirt, loose bark and soft rot, then soak for several days.
A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng recommends boiling for about 1-2 hours, repeated with water changes until the boiling water is no longer deep yellow.
A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng says to change the soaking water daily or every other day; large pieces may need several weeks.
A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng advises against boiling, saying it can break down the wood's structure and speed up rotting.
The same guide says soaking can take from several days to 1-2 weeks, and shop-bought wood is usually pre-treated but may still need soaking if it floats.
A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng says wood that still floats should be soaked longer or weighed down with stones until it is waterlogged.
Aqua Mart says lũa kim sa tùng suits tying moss and making bonsai-style arrangements.
Brothers Concept presents it as decor for freshwater aquariums and planted tanks.
The terrarium shop says it suits tropical terrariums with moss and ferns, semi-arid terrariums with succulents and cacti, and Tillandsia attached to the wood.
A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng says moss, Anubias (ráy), ferns, Bucephalandra and other rhizome plants attach well to driftwood.
General driftwood guides that do not name sa tùng warn that sharp, pointed branches can tear the fins of long-finned fish such as bettas and guppies.
In damp terrariums, mold or algae can form on the surface; the terrarium shop advises regular checks and scrubbing with a soft brush.

A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng lists these mistakes: skipping preparation, then blaming the wood for yellow water or mold; putting new wood in the tank right after buying it; and choosing a piece for its looks without checking it fits the tank.
The same guide warns against hiding the wood under too many plants and against crowding several pieces into a small tank.
A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng warns against cleaning driftwood with soap or chemical cleaners.
Zen Aquarius sells lũa kim sa tùng by the kilogram (1 kg).
Aqua Mart, in Bắc Từ Liêm, Hà Nội, lists lũa kim sa tùng.
Bống Vàng sells Lũa Kim sa tùng in 1 kg lots, in its Cát-Sỏi-Đá-Lũa category.
Brothers Concept lists Lũa Sa Tùng Cổ Thụ Gốc, which was out of stock at the time.
Brothers Concept's Lũa Sa Tùng Cổ Thụ Nhánh page was out of stock and gave no size specifications.
Thái Hoà Aquarium lists Lũa Sa Tùng among the driftwood types it supplies.
A general driftwood guide that does not name sa tùng advises choosing firm, well-aged wood with little rot and no fresh sap.
The same guide advises avoiding soft, spongy wood or wood with an unusual smell, and checking for cracks, crumbling areas and mold.
The same guide advises choosing a shape and size that fit the tank, and deciding first whether the piece will be the focal point, a branch for plants or a base for rocks.
